extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of literature; aspiring poets and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on choosing and developing a poetic subject that supplies natural continuity and unity, allows room for description, incident, and reflection, and is composed from close sensory observation; plus related guidance on persuasive political writing and literary study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject must supply natural connection and unity to the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a subject that 'supply in itself a natural connection to the parts, and unity to the whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge criticises THE TASK for lacking such a subject and therefore having weak structural cohesion. He gives the example of tracing a stream from source to fall to sea as a subject that naturally connects parts and gives unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject should give equal room for description, incident, and impassioned reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a subject that 'should give equal room and freedom for description, incident, and impassioned reflections on men, nature, and society.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning a poem, ensure the subject accommodates multiple modes (descriptive detail, narrative incident, and moral or passionate reflection) so the various parts of the poem have a natural role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid awkward connections and abrupt, arbitrary transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware that 'the connections are frequently awkward, and the transitions abrupt and arbitrary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is given as an explicit anti-pattern (critique of THE TASK). Ensure smooth, logically motivated transitions between sections so the reader perceives continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustain the subject throughout the work (do not abandon it after opening pages)
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong poem carries its central subject beyond the first few pages; Coleridge notes the defect that 'the subject... was not, and indeed could not be, carried on beyond the three or four first pages.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing a subject, test whether it can be sustained for the intended length; avoid subjects that only suit a brief introductory section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose from immediate sensory observation and make preparatory studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Work 'with my pencil and memorandum-book in my hand, ... making studies, as the artists call them, and often moulding my thoughts into verse, with the objects and imagery immediately before my senses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fieldwork, sketches, and immediate sensory notes to generate concrete imagery and keep description grounded in observed detail rather than abstract generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a subject that provides a structural metaphor or tracing (e.g., a stream)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a subject that permits a natural, progressive tracing (Coleridge's example: a stream traced from its source to the seaport) to provide room for varied material and an organizing principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A physically or narratively progressive subject offers an implicit structure for description, incident, and reflection, aiding unity and development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground political or persuasive writing in principles rather than mere passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective political writing 'referred habitually to principles' — Burke is praised as a 'scientific statesman' who bases arguments on principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argumentative or polemical pieces gain long-term authority and prophetic power when they appeal to enduring principles rather than transient facts or partisan rhetoric; this may make them tedious to contemporaries but lasting in value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid censurable or inappropriate uses of scripture/mottos that alienate readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge notes that an 'essay against fast days, with a most censurable application of a text from Isaiah for its motto, lost me near five hundred of my subscribers at one blow.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful in selecting epigraphs, mottoes, or scriptural applications: a poorly chosen or offensive use can alienate readership and harm reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep reading and linguistic/literary study inform and strengthen composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge describes extensive study of German language and literature (Gothic, Minnesinger, Pindar, Chaucer, Dante, Milton, etc.) as part of his formation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate knowledge of literary tradition and languages; close study of predecessors and varied literatures supplies forms, themes, and techniques that enrich one’s own writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic genius is often associated with themes of liberty and reformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge observes 'instances of the close connection of poetic genius with the love of liberty and of genuine reformation' in writers from Pindar to Hans Sachs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or choosing themes for poetry, consider moral and political seriousness—engagement with liberty and reform has historically been linked to powerful poetic voices.
